overview: This file documents the State Department’s prolonged debate over approximately $80 million in gold held in Japan and earmarked during the war for French Indochina and Siam. The memoranda examine whether earmarking conveyed legal title, whether wartime collaboration or occupation invalidated the claims, whether the United States could act unilaterally, and whether the gold should instead support Japanese recovery, occupation costs, reparations, or compensation for all Japanese-occupied countries. They also reveal disagreement over the position to be taken before the Far Eastern Commission and the competing approaches of the State Department, Treasury, SCAP, and British authorities. The final personal correspondence between Kenneth P. Landon and Ambassador Edwin F. Stanton places the Siamese claim within the broader context of U.S.–Thai relations, Point IV assistance, military aid, anticommunism, and unstable Thai domestic politics.

subfiles.title: Memorandum seeking clearance of policy on French and Siamese gold
subfiles.to: FN, OPD, Le/E, SEA, FE, WE, NA, A-T, and A-S
subfiles.about: Requests formal departmental approval of a proposed letter to the Army establishing how the French and Siamese gold claims should be handled.
subfiles.summary: Whitman reports agreement that unilateral action is inadvisable and that the dispute should be referred to the Far Eastern Commission. The proposed course called for the United States initially to withhold a position and decide later in light of proposals from other FEC members. A draft letter to General Draper and minutes of the December 1 meeting are identified as attachments.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser’s objection to withholding an initial FEC position
subfiles.about: Challenges the proposal that the United States enter Far Eastern Commission consideration of the claims without an initial position.
subfiles.summary: Surrey accepts most conclusions of the December 1 discussion but rejects the suggestion that the United States might abstain from taking a position throughout the FEC debate. He argues that an initial position should be settled beforehand and that unresolved disagreements should be submitted to Under Secretary Lovett. On that basis, Le/E clears the communications intended for the French and Siamese governments.

subfiles.title: Wallner memorandum and Gross endorsement on the FEC impasse
subfiles.from: Woodruff Wallner, with endorsement by Ernest A. Gross
subfiles.about: Describes the internal impasse over the U.S. position and proposes a meeting between European and Far Eastern affairs officials.
subfiles.summary: Wallner argues that the United States turned to the FEC largely because it was reluctant to decide the claim unilaterally and therefore suggests allowing the FEC majority to shape the outcome without an initial U.S. position. He asks Reber to meet Walton Butterworth and settle the political disagreement between EUR and FE. Gross’s endorsement responds that the U.S. representative must nevertheless receive a formulated position or a set of fallback positions before deliberations begin.

subfiles.title: Status report on the Indochina gold claim
subfiles.about: Reviews the documentary and procedural history of the French Indochina claim and the effort to obtain a new legal opinion.
subfiles.summary: Fletcher records that France claimed 33,056.813 kilograms of fine gold earmarked at the Yokohama Specie Bank for the Bank of Indochina and later transferred to the Bank of Japan. He traces two French notes, unsent draft replies, and a legal opinion by Professor Hamel. Because the French and Siamese claims could not be separated, Fletcher and Robert B. Parke were preparing questions on whether the claims—or at least their post-Pearl Harbor portions—could legally be denied and whether the United States could decide the matter without the FEC. He also asks that the legal opinion address the first charge principle and notes an enclosed policy paper intended for Thorp’s office.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the French and Siamese gold case papers
subfiles.about: Transmits ten notes, memoranda, legal submissions, and draft communications relating to the two gold claims.
subfiles.summary: Gohringer lists the assembled record of the dispute, including French notes, a Siamese note, draft replies, the December 1 memorandum of conversation, and memoranda involving Saltzman, Lovett, Surrey, Claxton, Butterworth, Gross, Wallner, and Reber. The package also contains Mr. Alk’s legal memorandum and drafts of a letter to General Draper. The document is useful as an inventory of the earlier administrative record.

subfiles.title: Policy survey of gold earmarked for Siam and French Indochina
subfiles.about: Explains the legal, political, reparations, and economic arguments governing the disposition of roughly $80 million in earmarked gold.
subfiles.summary: Whitman states that the gold comprised approximately $37 million for French Indochina and $43 million for Siam and that both governments were pressing SCAP for its release. Although the Legal Adviser and Treasury generally regarded earmarking as conveying title, OPD argued that post–December 7, 1941 transfers rewarded collaboration and discriminated against other occupied countries. Declaring the gold Japanese would make it available for reparations, Japanese foreign-trade financing, or potentially U.S. occupation costs under the disputed first charge principle; OE alternatively favored distribution among all former Japanese-occupied countries. FN, by contrast, leaned toward recognizing the claimants’ ownership subject to FEC review, while a working group prepared further legal questions before an office-level decision.

subfiles.title: Draft request for a Legal Adviser’s opinion
subfiles.about: Requests legal opinions on the first charge principle and on treating the earmarked French Indochinese and Siamese gold as Japanese property.
subfiles.summary: The draft contrasts the U.S. interpretation of FEC policies protecting occupation costs with the British view that Japanese-owned gold had already been made available for reparations. It sets out the policy case for invalidating post–December 7, 1941 earmarkings because they arose from wartime commercial and military arrangements under Japanese occupation. Evidence from Japanese ministries suggested that officials themselves disagreed over when title passed, while Japan’s refusal to ship some earmarked gold and its payment of insurance and transport costs further complicated the title question. The memorandum also asks whether Treasury would purchase the gold after a unilateral or FEC denial of the claims and whether equitable distribution among former Japanese-occupied countries would be legally defensible.

subfiles.title: Stanton letter on Siamese gold, Point IV, and Thai politics
subfiles.from: Edwin F. Stanton, American Embassy, Bangkok
subfiles.about: Warns of the diplomatic cost of withholding Siam’s gold while discussing technical aid and political instability in Siam.
subfiles.summary: Stanton welcomes Landon’s efforts to bring the gold issue to the Secretary and warns that Siamese opinion would regard U.S. retention of the gold for Japanese occupation costs as robbery. He reports SCAP’s objections and divergent British Foreign Office and Treasury attitudes, noting that Mr. Doll would seek British support in the FEC. Stanton then discusses the design and publicity of Point IV assistance and argues that aid could strengthen Siamese resistance to communism. He also describes tension between the Army and Navy, the Phibun government’s campaign against Pridi’s followers, the power of Kat’s coup group, and the possibility of further coups.

subfiles.title: Landon reply on enemy assets, military aid, and Point IV
subfiles.about: Replies on Stanton’s health and reviews Siamese enemy assets, reimbursable military assistance, family news, and the prospective Point IV program.
subfiles.summary: Landon urges Stanton to seek consultation or treatment in the United States if his health requires it and warns discreetly that Jimmy Scott is interested in his post. He reports an impending Siamese request for the United States to leave its joint trust with Britain over enemy assets and describes his efforts to keep reimbursable military aid for Siam before Congress. After extensive family news, he explains that Point IV would require new legislation beyond the Smith-Mundt Act and was independent of a Fulbright agreement. He adds that Siam had one of the strongest proposed programs east of India, although President Truman preferred to channel as much aid as possible through the United Nations.

interest: The file is especially valuable for showing how an apparently technical question of property title became entangled with reparations, occupation finance, Japanese economic recovery, wartime collaboration, and postwar diplomacy. The competing internal memoranda expose sharp disagreement over whether law should control policy and preserve the earmarks or whether equity toward other occupied countries justified confiscation or redistribution. Evidence that Japanese ministries themselves disputed when title passed offers unusual insight into the mechanics of wartime gold transactions. Stanton and Landon’s personal letters then reveal the prospective political cost in Siam and connect the dispute to early Cold War aid, military policy, anticommunism, and Thai political instability.
